course_description:
How should organisations and entrepreneurs decide what to innovate and when? This course introduces a strategic approach to innovation in the context of dynamic markets and increasing uncertainty, enabling you to understand innovation as a manageable process. It covers key frameworks and techniques to support decision‑making throughout the innovation journey, including innovating business models and technologies, managing innovation projects and portfolios, leveraging diverse sources of innovation, and formulating timely and effective innovation strategies.

EIBS7302 explores how organisations and entrepreneurs can strategically manage innovation in environments characterised by rapid technological change and uncertainty. The course is built around a central idea: innovation is not simply the result of inventiveness or luck, but a process that can be deliberately designed, evaluated, and managed over time.

You will engage with core topics including technological and business model innovation management, innovation processes and portfolios, open and collaborative innovation strategies, platforms and ecosystems, organisational and network dynamics, and go-to-market strategies. These capabilities are highly transferable across entrepreneurial ventures, innovation‑driven organisations, consulting, and technology‑intensive industries.

The course combines structured frameworks, applied cases, interactive discussions, and group‑based activities. You are expected to actively contribute insights from your own professional, and cultural perspectives. The course equips you with employability‑relevant capabilities, including strategic judgment, analytical thinking, and decision‑making skills applicable across entrepreneurial and innovation‑driven settings..

Course Changes in Response to Previous Student Feedback

Assessment 2 has been redesigned around a more authentic task that draws on the strategic decisions you make throughout the simulation.

assessment_details.task_description: What do you need to do? Blogging is the process of sharing your thoughts about a particular subject on a social media platform. Many professionals use it to establish their knowledge, build credibility, and engage with an audience. For this assessment, you will create your own blog on the EIBS7302 blogging platform on learn.uq.edu.au to share your thoughts on innovation. Think of it as starting a conversation with your peers about how you see innovation and what makes it interesting to you. Your own blog needs to use real-world examples and explain them in light of the weekly course topics to your peers. You and your peers will also engage in conversations with each other by commenting on each other’s blog posts. The goal is to: Create a community of thinkers focused on innovation; Make intangible innovation concepts from the course tangible and applicable in the real world; Learn to communicate and present ideas professionally; and, most importantly, Have fun! How do you need to do it? Your own blog must build on concepts from the course and be structured as follows: Part 1 (500-800 words): Kick-off your blog with a post about why you are interested in innovation. This post should introduce your personal story and explain why innovation is important for you based on an illustrative real-world example. Part 2 (350-500 words per post): For at least four of the twelve weeks, add new posts to your blog to continue establishing your knowledge and building credibility in your area of interest. Every post should feature a real-world example that is aligned with your personal interest and discuss and analyse this example in light of one of the weekly topics. Think of these posts as the puzzle pieces that all together tell others why you are knowledgeable and credible in your area of interest. As part of this assessment, you will also need to engage with and comment on blog posts of your peers. This will create a community of thinkers focused on innovation and ensure that everyone in the course has an audience for his or her blog. Part 3 (120-200 words per post): For at least five of the twelve weeks, make constructive comments on blog posts of your peers. It is important that you make at least ten comments in total. For example, you could comment on two blogs posts each for five weeks, or you could comment on one blog post each for ten weeks. In your comments, you can add additional insights to your peers’ posts, explain why some information in their posts is particularly revelatory, and even constructively challenge the posts of your peers. Important is that your argumentation is professional, clearly substantiated, and advances the conversation. The expectation is that the blogs will be evidence-based. For this reason, each post on your own blog needs to contain at least one link to a source where your information comes from (e.g., news article, corporate homepage, academic article, etc.). This also applies to comments on your peers’ blog posts if your comments should introduce new information. How do you present this information? You are free to be creative and can choose how you want to create and present the blog posts and comments. Important is that each post: Focuses on a specific course topic; Has a clear line of argumentation with a beginning, middle, and end; and Communicates coherently, consistently and cohesively in a professional manner. Overall, your blog posts need to be able to stand alone, explain and situate innovation in light of the course topics, and create a conversation around your chosen area of interest. In turn, because we want to build a community of innovation thinkers, your comments on your peers’ blog posts need to explicitly tie into their posts and conversations and be written in light of the course topics too. assessment_details.task_description: What do you need to do? This assessment focuses on implementing strategies to navigate disruptive innovation. You will need to play the Back Bay Battery simulation game which Professor Christensen developed to simulate the real-life challenges of making investment decisions between mature and emerging technologies under uncertainty. You will receive the link to the simulation three weeks in advance. Within the three-week period, you will be able to complete 6 simulation runs at different difficulty scenarios at your own pace. For the last run in Advanced scenario, you will need to hand-write a decision log (template provided in Blackboard), documenting your strategic moves during that run. After the three-week period, you will need to write up your reflection during a 60-minute class scheduled for completing the assessment. No devices or aids in any form will be allowed in class, except for your decision log which you will need to hand over together with the reflection. Note that the decision log itself will not be assessed. How do you need to do it? Your written reflection must address a series of questions, presented during class, that relate to the strategy you implemented in the simulation, the market changes that forced you to adapt, how course concepts help explain your experience, and what you learned from the activity in relation to our course. Importantly, your mark will not be influenced by whether you succeed in the simulation game or not. What matters is that you draw on the concepts and approaches covered in weeks 1-7 to reflect on the strategies you used during the simulation. How do you present this information? Your reflection needs to be understandable by others. Therefore, it is important to communicate your responses coherently, consistently and cohesively. This means that your report needs to be: Precise and logically structured; and Provide insightful and convincing explanations Why do you need to reflect? The act of reflection provides us with signposted moments to stop, think about the bigger picture and synthesise information. When you reflect on your simulation experience, you discuss what you would do differently (or the same way) and why. Documenting your decisions in a log or journal is a practice used by many innovation practitioners and entrepreneurs. It proves effective for learning which strategies worked and which did not, and it serves as evidence when you later need to justify your decisions to peers, managers, or a board. Disruptive innovation, the lens for this simulation, was developed by Professor Clayton Christensen at Harvard Business School. His work explained why successful firms can fail when confronted with disruptive technological change, and how organisations might respond strategically. If you are unsure of what disruptive innovation is, you can read the first chapter of his book . Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Self-written case study
assessment_details.task_description: What do you need to do? You need to write a case study—similar to the Harvard cases we used in class but shorter—about a real-world innovation example (i.e., a specific innovation, organisation, or industry) to teach others about innovation strategy and innovation management. You are required to pick one of the course's subjects, identify and gather information about a real-world example of your choice that allows you to discuss this subject, and analyse the example with the concepts and techniques from the course. The selected example must be different from the cases discussed in class, unless you analyse it through a completely different lens. The overall goal is to demonstrate that you understand a complex innovation strategy and innovation management subject well enough to be able to explain it to others in an accessible way. How do you need to do it? Your case study should be no longer than 2,000 words and contain the following elements: An introduction of the case study that creates interest A background section that provides insights into the case study's business environment A core analysis section that provides insights into the focal subject based on the case study A conclusion section that summarises the lessons learnt from the case study A list of references (not included in the word count) How do you present it? Your case study needs to communicate coherently, consistently and cohesively to enable others to learn about the focal subject. It is important that you distinguish between the significant—all the information you need to explain the focal subject—and the trivial—all the information that do not really matter for your analysis and only distract readers. Therefore, your case study needs to be: Precise and logically structured; Only include significant information; Identify trustworthy sources that others could use to validate or reject the case study information; and be Professionally presented, which includes consistent referencing of sources in APA style.
